summary: The sign-in server now records which applications an account was actually let into. Until now its history showed that somebody signed in and stopped there — which is only half the story, because signing in happens once and the access it is then traded for happens separately for every application. If an account were ever misused, the question you would need answered is which systems it reached, and this was the one component that knew and did not write it down. Refusals are recorded too, and are arguably the more useful half: an attempt to have somebody's sign-in sent to an address that was never registered, a request from an application nobody has registered, or a one-time code being used a second time are exactly what an attack on this looks like, and a history containing only successes cannot show one.
compatibility: Purely additive: nothing about signing in changes, and no configuration or migration is needed. The new entries appear in the existing audit screen and its CSV export alongside the sign-in records, and can be filtered by name like any other action. Recording is best-effort by design — if the history cannot be written the sign-in still proceeds, because refusing to let somebody in because a log line failed would turn a reporting problem into an outage. Worth knowing when reading old history: entries before this release will show sign-ins with no matching record of which application followed, because that was never captured.
